newsitem.title: USA: Justice Dept. announces Columbia/HCA charges.
newsitem.headline: Justice Dept. announces Columbia/HCA charges.

text.p: Three Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. executives have been charged with fraud in the first charges from the government investigation of the nation's largest for-profit hospital chain, the Justice Department said Wednesday.

It said a federal grand jury in Florida indicted the executives on five counts alleging conspiracy to submit false cost reports under U.S. heath care programmes, Medicare fraud and making false statements.
"This indictment ... represents the first phase of the government's ongoing investigation" of Columbia, U.S. Attorney Charles Wilson in Florida said in a statement.

Indicted were Jay Jarrell, chief executive of Columbia's southwest Florida division; Michael Neeb, chief financial officer of its northern Florida division, and Robert Whiteside, director of reimbursement at its Nashville, Tenn., headquarters.
Each defendant faces up to 25 years in prison and fines up to $1.25 million if convicted.

They were charged with conspiring to submit false costs reports under Medicare and the military's Civilian Health and Medical Programme on behalf of Fawcett Memorial Hospital in Port Charlotte, Fla., from 1986 until June.
The indictment was returned June 25 but not made public until Wednesday. The Justice Department in Washington made available a copy of the indictment and Wilson's statement announcing the charges.
Wilson said the indictment had been returned before the recent searches of various Columbia and related facilities in Florida and other states.

Earlier this month, federal agents raided 35 Columbia facilities in six states and seized files. In addition, five mid-level executives were subpoenaed in a broad inquiry into possible improper billing for laboratory tests, home health care and Medicare-related work.
The investigation led to the resignation under fire Friday of long-time Columbia Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Richard Scott, as well as President David Vandewater.

Dr. Thomas Frist, formerly vice chairman, replaced Scott as chairman and CEO. Frist has said he intends to compile a plan to change the company over the next week or so, take it to the Justice Department for review and ask for 90 to 100 days to implement it.
U.S. Attorney Wilson described the case as "an important part of my office's commitment to fight against alleged fraud and abuse in our health care system."

In Fort Myers, Jarrell, one of the indicted executives, appeared before a federal magistrate for a hearing that a court clerk called an "initial appearance" at which the charges were read. An arraignment and bond hearing will be scheduled later.
